newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND-Reform key for Latam success in 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Reform key for Latam success in 1997.

text.p: Investors in Latin America usually expect politics to give them a bumpy ride but economic and political reforms make the region attractive for 1997, with Brazil likely to be at the top of investor shopping lists.
Economists predict four percent average GDP growth for Latam in 1997 and say it has greater opportunities than southeast Asia where the growth story is running out of steam.
"Overall the reform trend is continuing on the right track and I am optimistic on the region next year," one Latin American fund manager said.
"What you're seeing is accelerating (GDP) growth, higher earnings growth than Asia and higher multiples."
"Any surprises are likely to be more in the political arena next year," said Joe McHatton, chief Latin American strategist at Kleinwort Benson.

Economists stress the importance of Latin America sticking to the now well defined path for emerging economies -- improving their tax systems, opening up and freeing trade, privatising, and implementing fiscal discipline.

"If you follow this model the markets will reward you and your economy will reward you," said one, adding Chile was almost of the end of this process, Argentina was 75 percent of the way there, while Brazil and Mexico had furthest to go.

The pressure will be on Brazil in particular to take the crucial legislative steps toward slashing its unwieldy budget deficit and preserving the gains already made under its inflation-fighting currency, the real.
But the chances of that hinge more and more on constitutional change to allow free market President Fernando Henrique Cardoso a second term to complete the laborious reform process.
"Brazil is still very cheap compared with the rest of the region," said Kleinwort Benson's McHatton.

"Earnings are climbing rapidly, mainly because companies are being better managed, and their value is increasing with economic growth, with the increase in consumer spending and the rationalisation of many state controlled firms."

Latin America's biggest privatisation to date, the sell-off of Brazilian mining giant CVRD, will go ahead in 1997 once haggling over the use of the proceeds is resolved. But not all investors are excited.

"It is important in terms of Brazil's fiscal revenues, but as a stock it is probably one of the less attractive," said one Latam fund manager here. "It is not a clear cut Brazilian story -- it is more an international commodity story."
Instead she was looking to a pick-up in growth in Argentina next year for specific sector plays.
"The domestic recovery story should give opportunities in banking, construction, retail and steel, and there will be a few natural resource plays like (oil firm) Astra," she said.
On the negative side for Latam, strategists at UBS, in a quarterly outlook published in November, expressed worries over the region's trade balance.
"Less favourable is our expectation that the trade picture will worsen next year as import growth in Argentina and Brazil pushes the regional trade balance into deficit," it said.

Kleinwort's McHatton pointed to negative feedback into the economy from Colombia's crackdown on guerrillas and drug lords, while Mexico could feel the pinch from more active rebel movements and increased pressure for higher real wages.

Mexico seems destined to wait out in the cold until its domestic economy recovers from its 1995 financial crisis. Analysts, however, say Latam's financial sector will perform well in 1997 due to its participation in the region's growth, as will retailers in most markets, though more modestly in Mexico.
The electricity sector would be a laggard in most areas -- except in Brazil due to restructuring ahead of privatisation.
But several analysts tipped telecoms as Latam's big winner.
"Telecoms in general will continue to do well -- most of them are in Brazil -- in terms of numbers and size they dominate the region," said one.
ING Barings agreed, seeing the Brazilian telecom sector benefitting from a phase of impressive growth. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
